name: Aldabra Atoll
blurb: Giant tortoises, coconut crabs and frigatebirds on a remote coral atoll.

tip.title: Remove the tortoises
tip.text: About 100,000 giant tortoises graze the turf and scrub. Lower their numbers and watch the tortoise turf, land crabs, coconut crabs and the flightless rail respond.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae in the lagoon and the surrounding sea. They feed corals, flying fish and the rest of the open-water web.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: Meadows in the shallow lagoon that green turtles graze.

nodes.name: Mangroves
nodes.desc: Aldabra has seven mangrove species lining the lagoon edge, forming a key part of the coastal ecosystem.

nodes.name: Tortoise turf
nodes.desc: A short mix of grasses and herbs, dwarfed by constant grazing, that grows in the tortoises' pastures.

nodes.name: Pemphis scrub
nodes.desc: Dense shrub that covers much of the higher, rocky ground of the atoll.

nodes.name: Aldabra giant tortoise
nodes.desc: About 100,000 live here, the largest population anywhere. They eat grasses, leaves and woody stems, and like elephants they shape the landscape.

nodes.name: Land crabs
nodes.desc: Burrowing crabs of the mangrove and scrub fringe that eat leaf litter. They also prey on young tortoises.

nodes.name: Reef-building corals
nodes.desc: Hard corals on the outer reefs and in the lagoon. Bleaching in 2016 cut hard coral cover on seaward reefs by over half, and juveniles have since returned.

nodes.name: Flying fish
nodes.desc: Plankton-feeding fish of the open sea. They are the most common prey of great frigatebirds.

nodes.name: Green turtle
nodes.desc: Nests on Aldabra in large numbers. Adults graze seagrass and algae in the shallow lagoon.

nodes.name: Hawksbill turtle
nodes.desc: Lives on reefs and eats sponges, corals and other invertebrates. Breeds on the atoll.

nodes.name: Aldabra rail
nodes.desc: The last flightless bird of the Indian Ocean region, a flightless form of the white-throated rail found here.

nodes.name: Red-footed booby
nodes.desc: Nests in the trees and shrubs and hunts flying fish and squid at sea.

nodes.name: Great frigatebird
nodes.desc: Breeds here in large numbers (subspecies aldabrensis). Snatches flying fish from the sea surface and sometimes steals food from other seabirds.

nodes.name: Great barracuda
nodes.desc: Fast predator of the reefs and lagoon edges, hunting other fish.

nodes.name: Coconut crab
nodes.desc: The largest land arthropod. It eats fruit and carrion and also kills tortoise hatchlings and other crabs. Adults have almost no predators.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: Top predator of the surrounding sea. It takes turtles of all sizes as well as fish.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun drives growth in the lagoon, on the reef and on land.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Fresh water is scarce, and tortoises take most of their moisture from their food. Rain sets how well the turf and scrub grow.

nodes.name: Tidal lagoon
nodes.desc: A large, shallow lagoon of seagrass, mudflats and mangroves that empties and refills with the tides.

nodes.name: Limestone soil
nodes.desc: A thin soil over raised coral limestone that holds the turf, scrub and mangrove roots.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and small invertebrates that break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.
